narrative:
The model that reviewed your application concluded that you have a 54% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. This means the strongest prediction, based on your academic record, was that failure was slightly more likely than success. That is why your application was denied—the school relies on this prediction to admit students it believes will pass, and you fell just on the wrong side of that line.

The single most influential factor in that decision was your LSAT score. At 18, your score is drastically below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, and this had the largest impact on the model. It pushed your prediction decisively toward failing the bar, and no other factor came close to overriding it.

Two other factors mattered, but they worked in your favor. Your first-year class standing placed you in the 7th decile, which is better than the 6th-decile average of admitted students, and this nudged the prediction slightly toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, though below the admitted average of 3.23, also contributed modestly toward a passing outcome because of how it interacted with the model. However, both of these positive influences were much weaker than the negative weight of your LSAT score, so they could not compensate for it.

To improve your chances, focus almost entirely on raising your LSAT score. This one number was the decisive factor against you, and significant preparation or a retake would directly address the model's largest concern. Strong improvement here could flip a future prediction in your favor.
